articles.title: Some people are resistant to dementia — here’s what their genes can teach us
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03625-8For years, researchers have studied people with a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer’s and other dementias. They might have even more to learn from those who don’t get the disease.
articles.content:
The ravages of age touch us all — some more lightly than others. Geneticist Henne Holstege wanted to study people with a particular superpower: those resistant to neurodegeneration, despite their age or their genes putting them at high risk.

Brains of ‘super agers’ are strong producers of new neurons

At first, she struggled to get funders interested. “For five years, all my grants were rejected,” she recalls. “Each time was a cup of poison.”

But she persevered, convinced that these super-agers could help scientists to understand why a privileged few people manage to avoid conditions such as neurodegeneration, which ail so many in older age.

She finally launched her project in 2013, and ever since, Holstege and others in her field have uncovered a rash of gene variants that seem to protect against dementias.

Researchers are increasingly convinced that understanding resilience to dementia is just as interesting as the more familiar genetics of high risk.

The brain, it seems, has its own defence mechanisms against the toxic proteins that cause Alzheimer’s — mechanisms that scientists now hope to exploit.

They think that protective gene variants will help to illuminate how the disease emerges and worsens — and potentially how to treat it. Of particular interest is a group of variants that affect the workings of the ApoE protein (apolipoprotein E), which carries fat molecules essential for cellular function. Some forms of this protein are long-known contributors to the risk of Alzheimer’s. But some recently discovered and rare variants seem to confer resistance.

“Nature has already done the experiment for us: certain gene variants protect us from Alzheimer’s and they do so safely,” says neuroscientist Guojun Bu from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. “Learning how they do this could guide us to new therapies.”

Impervious to plaques

The relentless course of Alzheimer’s disease follows a decades-long progression that is kick-started when amyloid-β proteins in the brain clump into plaques. It concludes with loss of synapses and death of brain cells.

Except when it doesn’t. Just occasionally, people whose brains are full of plaques don’t follow the usual route. They stay free of dementia for most or all of their long lives. A few people don’t even build plaques, even though some might carry gene variants conferring a high Alzheimer’s risk.

In the brain of a person with Alzheimer’s disease (right), amyloid-β proteins clump into plaques, as shown in a magnetic-resonance-imaging scan.Credit: Mark & Mary Stevens Neuroimaging & Informatics Inst./SPL

In the normal course of disease, the amyloid-β proteins in plaques activate immune cells in the brain known as microglia, which try to clear them. But if active for too long, the microglia become inflammatory and start to damage neurons. This, along with other cellular stresses, promotes the build-up and spread of a different, deadlier type of protein, called tau, which forms long, thin tangles. These tangles correlate with the development and severity of dementia symptoms.

Although lifestyle and environmental factors can affect the likelihood of developing the disease, the most powerful influence is genetics.

The exact mechanistic details of how plaques lead to symptoms are still unclear. Gene variants that either accelerate or slow disease could affect many pathways. One such pathway might relate directly to clearance of toxic amyloids or spreading of tau, but could also be acting indirectly, by affecting energy systems in brain cells, for example. “That’s why it is important to identify these variants and discover their exact mechanisms,” says Holstege, who is at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

Searching the genome

The search for gene mutations that contribute to the risk of Alzheimer’s goes back decades. A small number of Alzheimer’s cases are strongly hereditary, involving mutations in genes that result in a higher proportion of stickier, toxic forms of amyloid-β proteins. Just one copy of any of these mutated genes almost inevitably leads to disease development early in adult life, most often when someone is in their 40s or 50s.

How to avoid dementia — what the science really says

However, familial early-onset Alzheimer’s accounts for fewer than 1% of all cases; most cases affect people over 65. The APOE gene is the most important genetic determinant of the late-onset form of disease. The protein it encodes, ApoE, is central to lipid transport between cells and around the body. If it does its job properly, it can help to prevent amyloid build-up and clear it from the brain; it can also influence tau pathology, partly through effects on microglia.

Three main alleles of the gene exist, which generate a spectrum of risk. The alleles differ from each other in only one or two nucleotide positions. APOE3 is the most common variant. APOE4 dials the risk up and is the greatest genetic risk factor known. “The particular nucleotide substitution makes the protein it encodes more likely to aggregate and less likely to do its day job of transporting lipids,” says Bu. APOE2 dials the risk down: two copies can delay onset of Alzheimer’s by a decade. Only about 1% of the population has two copies of APOE2.

But however notable the effects of APOE alleles, the vast majority of late-onset Alzheimer cases result from the combined effects of many, often rare, gene variants — some increasing and others reducing disease risk — as well as short stretches of DNA that influence how much each gene is expressed.

Scientists have so far identified only part of the genetic contribution to Alzheimer’s risk. They think that the missing genetics — including numerous but rare variants — might hold some of the most biologically informative clues about resilience.

A controversial Alzheimer’s surgery is said to reverse symptoms — here’s what scientists know

The usual way to search for variants is in genome-wide association studies (GWAS), in which scientists analyse millions of spots on the genome for differences between groups — for example, those with disease or at high risk of disease, compared with those who are disease-free or cognitively resilient. These spots are called single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). A SNP can act as a flag for a stretch of DNA that looks different in high-risk individuals than in those who are cognitively resilient.

To search for extremely rare resilience genes, you need sequences from huge numbers of people and sensitive identification techniques. Both have improved in the past decade or so. Hundreds of thousands of genomes from people with and without Alzheimer’s are available from sources such as UK Biobank. “The more people you look at, the more likely you are to spot very rare occurrences,” says Michael Greicius, a geneticist at Stanford University in California.

New cohorts are being put together all the time, and those that include people of Asian, African and other ancestry show significant differences in Alzheimer’s risk genetics compared with predominantly European-ancestry cohorts1.

Greicius’s team has found a rare protective variant known as W276C in a population of people with Native American ancestry, which has not been seen in the other cohorts2. “There’s an incredible amount of power in ancestrally diverse data sets that we miss completely when we myopically focus on European ancestry,” he says.

Not-so-sticky proteins

Once candidate resilience variants have been identified in human genetic studies, scientists begin the lengthy task of working out whether — and how — they might affect disease biology. They mutate these genes in mice or cell cultures and also look for cells or biological pathways that have been affected in donated brain tissue.

A dozen or so rare gene variants have now been verified in this way as likely contributors to Alzheimer’s resilience, although the strength of evidence varies greatly between them. APOE itself has produced some of the clearest examples. Three extremely rare variants of APOE3 have been found in people who seem to escape Alzheimer’s, and one variant of APOE4 seems to neutralize the risk usually carried by that form. All of them are gold dust for scientists. “These rare variants hold the key to understanding how the common risk variants do what they do,” says biochemist Rosie Jackson at the University of Dundee, UK.

The changes to the protein might be tiny, but the consequences are huge. They all affect how the ApoE protein binds to molecules.

ApoE is shaped a bit like a hairpin (see ‘Protective protein’). One arm has surfaces that attract and carry lipids. Once a lipid is bound, the protein opens up and reshapes itself around it. The other arm binds to receptors on cells, allowing those cells to ingest ApoE and use its lipid cargo. These receptors can also take up tau and contribute to its spread between cells.

There are three rare variants found in the APOE3 allele. One is known as the Christchurch variant (after the city in New Zealand in which it was discovered) and it affects the receptor-binding region of the ApoE protein. It is thought to bind ApoE less strongly to receptors, making tau less likely to spread.

The other two rare APOE3 variants influence the lipid-binding section, probably making the protein less sticky and less likely to clump and form plaques.

articles.personality_title: Scientists uncover genes that help protect some people from dementia
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Dementia, especially Alzheimer’s disease, affects millions of older people worldwide. While many develop the disease due to genetic risks or age, a small group of individuals, called "super-agers," remain free of dementia despite having high risk factors.

**What happened** – Geneticist Henne Holstege and her team studied these super-agers starting in 2013. They found rare gene variants that seem to protect the brain against dementia. One key focus is on the APOE gene, which controls a protein important for brain cell function. Some versions of this gene increase Alzheimer’s risk, but others reduce it or even prevent it. Scientists have identified several rare protective variants, including some that stop harmful protein clumps from spreading in the brain.

**Impact** – This research is important because it shows that nature already holds clues to resisting dementia. Understanding how protective genes work could lead to new treatments that help more people stay healthy as they age. It also highlights the value of studying diverse populations, since some protective genes are found only in certain groups.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue to study these rare gene variants to learn exactly how they protect the brain. They will use this knowledge to develop drugs or therapies that mimic the protective effects. Researchers are also expanding their studies to include people from different ancestries to discover more resilience genes.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By studying people who naturally resist dementia, scientists have found protective genes that could lead to new ways to prevent or treat Alzheimer’s disease.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
articles.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.
articles.content:
Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

The research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms."

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman says. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body."

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a company co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce important interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

The scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman says. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection."

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he says.

articles.title: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.
articles.content:
A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes?

Scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience.

Dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal.

The new research, published November 4 in Nature, examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed.

"We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

The findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better."

How the Gut Sends Reward Signals to the Brain

Scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention.

According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness.

When food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes.

To investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains.

The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food.

The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA.

The amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear.

"We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he said.

Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences

Finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors.

They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories.

The team then conducted the opposite experiment.

After mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward.

In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate.

Together, the experiments showed that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects.

A Surprising Discovery in the Left Side of the Brain

The researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern.

Dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories.

Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA.

A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar.

They observed increased activity in the same brain region.

One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres.

In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right.

That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion.

Why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference.

Could This Discovery Help Scientists Change Food Cravings?

Identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing?

One area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior.

Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the new study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified.

Still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors.

For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications.

The broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target.

By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry.

"By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight said.

The discovery offers a new perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about a gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that explains how food preferences develop over time, which has broad implications for understanding eating behavior and potential future treatments to reshape food cravings. The research is detailed, focused, and offers meaningful real-world benefits for public health by potentially influencing dietary habits and obesity-related issues.
articles.personality_title: Scientists uncover how the gut helps us learn to enjoy bitter coffee
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people find black coffee bitter and unpleasant at first. But over time, many learn to enjoy its taste. Scientists have wondered how our brains change to make us like flavors that we once disliked.

**What happened** – Researchers at the University of California, San Francisco discovered a slow dopamine pathway between the gut and the brain. Dopamine is a chemical in the brain that helps us learn and feel reward. By studying mice and reviewing human brain scans, they found that nutrients in the stomach send signals to the brain’s amygdala, a region involved in emotion and learning. These signals help the brain link certain tastes with positive effects, like caffeine’s boost from coffee.

**Impact** – This discovery explains why tastes like bitter coffee can become enjoyable after repeated experience. It also shows how the body’s digestive system talks to the brain to shape food preferences. Knowing this pathway could help scientists find new ways to change what foods people crave, possibly improving diets and health.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to learn why this dopamine signal is stronger on the brain’s left side and explore if certain medicines, like those affecting appetite, can change this gut-to-brain signal. This might lead to new treatments that help people develop healthier food preferences without just focusing on hunger.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists found a gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps the brain learn to like bitter flavors like coffee by linking taste with rewarding effects.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques découvrent comment l’intestin nous aide à aimer le café amer
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup de gens trouvent le café noir amer et désagréable au début. Mais avec le temps, ils apprennent à apprécier ce goût. Les scientifiques se demandaient comment notre cerveau change pour nous faire aimer des saveurs que nous n’aimions pas.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Californie à San Francisco ont découvert une voie lente de dopamine entre l’intestin et le cerveau. La dopamine est une substance chimique dans le cerveau qui nous aide à apprendre et à ressentir du plaisir. En étudiant des souris et en analysant des images du cerveau humain, ils ont trouvé que les nutriments dans l’estomac envoient des signaux à l’amygdale, une partie du cerveau liée aux émotions et à l’apprentissage. Ces signaux aident le cerveau à associer certains goûts à des effets positifs, comme la stimulation de la caféine.

**Impact** – Cette découverte explique pourquoi des goûts comme le café amer peuvent devenir agréables après plusieurs expériences. Elle montre aussi comment le système digestif communique avec le cerveau pour former nos préférences alimentaires. Comprendre cette voie pourrait aider à trouver de nouvelles façons de changer les envies alimentaires, ce qui pourrait améliorer les régimes et la santé.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent comprendre pourquoi ce signal de dopamine est plus fort dans la partie gauche du cerveau et étudier si certains médicaments, comme ceux qui agissent sur l’appétit, peuvent modifier ce signal entre l’intestin et le cerveau. Cela pourrait aboutir à de nouveaux traitements pour aider à développer des préférences alimentaires plus saines.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les scientifiques ont découvert une voie de dopamine entre l’intestin et le cerveau qui aide le cerveau à apprendre à aimer les saveurs amères comme le café en reliant le goût à des effets positifs.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren cómo el intestino nos ayuda a disfrutar el café amargo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas encuentran que el café negro es amargo y desagradable al principio. Pero con el tiempo, aprenden a disfrutar de su sabor. Los científicos se han preguntado cómo cambia el cerebro para que nos gusten sabores que antes no nos gustaban.

Estudiando ratones y revisando imágenes cerebrales humanas, encontraron que los nutrientes en el estómago envían señales a la amígdala, una parte del cerebro relacionada con las emociones y el aprendizaje. Estas señales ayudan al cerebro a conectar ciertos sabores con efectos positivos, como el estímulo de la cafeína.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento explica por qué sabores como el café amargo pueden volverse agradables después de probarlos varias veces. También muestra cómo el sistema digestivo habla con el cerebro para formar nuestras preferencias alimenticias. Conocer esta vía podría ayudar a los científicos a encontrar nuevas formas de cambiar los antojos de comida, mejorando la dieta y la salud.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren entender por qué esta señal de dopamina es más fuerte en el lado izquierdo del cerebro y explorar si ciertos medicamentos, como los que afectan el apetito, pueden cambiar esta señal del intestino al cerebro. Esto podría llevar a tratamientos nuevos para ayudar a las personas a desarrollar preferencias alimenticias más saludables.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos encontraron una vía de dopamina entre el intestino y el cerebro que ayuda al cerebro a aprender a gustar sabores amargos como el café, al conectar el sabor con efectos positivos.

articles.title: X chromosome gene may reduce autism rates in women and girls
articles.summary: A gene called ZFX exerts powerful effects on an entire network of genes linked to autism, which may help explain why the condition is less common in females
articles.content:
A gene called ZFX exerts powerful effects on an entire network of genes linked to autism, which may help explain why the condition is less common in females

The X chromosome seems to help reduce the chances of developing autism and we may be closer to understanding how nopparit/Getty Images

A single gene on the X chromosome may help explain why autism is less common in women and girls. The gene, ZFX, has powerful effects on a set of genes that contribute to the risk of autism, and is expressed more in women than in men.

“It’s about the fact that ZFX has a relationship with these other autism-associated genes,” says Rebecca Andersen, a neurogeneticist at Boston Children’s Hospital in Massachusetts. This one gene can keep other genes turned on when they might otherwise be deactivated, she says, reducing the chances that girls will develop autism.

Autism is a developmental condition. Autistic people have a variety of traits that can include difficulties with socialising and communicating, unusually high sensory sensitivity that can cause them to become overwhelmed, and restricted behaviours and interests.

Advertisement

Many studies have found that autism is more common in males than in females: up to four times as common. “That specific number is contested,” says Andersen, partly because we now know that autism presents differently in females, including subtler effects on socialising. Furthermore, women and girls with autism often “mask” or “camouflage” their autistic traits, enabling them to pass as neurotypical at the cost of their mental health. This means females often go undiagnosed, or are diagnosed later in life, skewing the figures.

Nevertheless, many autism researchers believe there is a “female protective effect”: something about being female makes people less likely to be autistic. Notably, women diagnosed with autism tend to have more autism-linked mutations than men diagnosed with autism. This suggests there is a requirement for a “greater genetic load in females in order to manifest with autism at all, or to manifest to a degree that would be diagnosed”, says Andersen.

Understanding this requires understanding the genetics of autism. “We’ve long known that there’s a very strong genetic component to autism,” says Andersen. “There have been a lot of large-scale sequencing studies that have identified hundreds of different genes that are implicated in autism,” she says. “It’s been really perplexing to understand how so many different genes could all be relevant for autism.”

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

To figure out how these genes work together, Andersen and her colleagues grew neural progenitor cells – which develop into neurons – in culture. They then targeted each of 20 genes, all known to be associated with autism. Rather than deleting or mutating the genes, they used a version of the CRISPR gene-editing technology to break down the RNA produced when the genes were expressed. Reduced expression of these genes is thought to increase the chances of developing autism. “We could target the RNA for degradation and have very rapid changes in expression levels of those genes,” says Andersen.

To their surprise, the researchers found that reducing the expression of any one of these genes tended to also significantly reduce the expression of most of the others. “Across almost all of our perturbations, they just looked very similar to one another, and in particular, how much they affected the other autism-associated genes,” says Andersen. “It seemed to make sense that they would have to converge in some way, in order to be related to autism, but we didn’t necessarily expect to find such a strong degree of convergence.”

The researchers then built a model of the interactions between the genes. This enabled them to identify a core of 70 genes, all of which strongly regulate the 20 autism-associated genes, and also regulate each other. Andersen calls these genes the “central hub”.

“This provides strong evidence that apparently distinct genetic causes of autism may converge on common pathways,” says Louise Gallagher at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, who wasn’t involved in the study.

Having identified these core genes, the team then identified a set of 82 genes that were expressed less when the autism-related genes were suppressed, and which are known to be more heavily expressed in female brains compared with male. This led the researchers to ZFX, which is found on the X chromosome. Females have two X chromosomes, but males have one X and a smaller Y chromosome. This means females have two copies of ZFX – and unusually for genes on the X chromosomes, both copies are expressed.

“We found that ZFX was very related to many of these different autism-associated genes,” says Andersen. This means ZFX could act as a buffer. A girl could have a lot of mutations that reduce the expression of autism-associated genes and thus increase her probability of autism – only for the ZFX to increase the expression of those genes and reduce her chances of autism.

“That’s very interesting and biologically plausible,” says Gallagher. However, the claim rests on the team’s model of the interactions between the genes. “The paper doesn’t show that increasing ZFX expression rescues the consequences of the variants.” That would require additional experiments.

“It’s also unlikely that something as complex as the female protective effect will be attributable to a single gene,” says Gallagher. “It could be related to other sex-linked genetic mechanisms, hormonal influences and broader differences in developmental biology.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery identifying a gene (ZFX) on the X chromosome that may help explain why autism is less common in females. This finding provides meaningful insight into autism genetics, potentially advancing understanding and future treatments, which has broad implications for health and developmental research.
articles.personality_title: Gene on X chromosome may explain why fewer girls have autism
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Autism is a condition that affects how people communicate and behave. It is diagnosed more often in boys than in girls. Scientists have wondered why girls seem to be protected from autism more than boys.

**What happened** – Researchers found a gene called ZFX on the X chromosome that could help explain this difference. Girls have two X chromosomes and two copies of this gene, while boys have only one. ZFX helps control other genes linked to autism, keeping them active when they might otherwise be turned off.

**Impact** – This discovery shows how many different genes related to autism work together. The ZFX gene acts like a “buffer” in girls, lowering the chance they will develop autism even if they have mutations in other genes. This helps explain why autism is less common in females and points to new ways of studying the condition.

**What’s next step** – Scientists will need to do more experiments to confirm how ZFX protects against autism. They also want to explore other factors like hormones or additional genes that might play a role. The goal is to better understand autism’s causes and improve diagnosis and treatment.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A gene on the X chromosome, ZFX, may help protect girls from autism by controlling other autism-related genes and keeping them active.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un gène du chromosome X pourrait expliquer pourquoi moins de filles ont l'autisme
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

Les filles ont deux chromosomes X et donc deux copies de ce gène, tandis que les garçons n'en ont qu'une. ZFX aide à contrôler d'autres gènes liés à l'autisme en les maintenant actifs.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre comment plusieurs gènes liés à l'autisme fonctionnent ensemble. Le gène ZFX agit comme un « tampon » chez les filles, réduisant leurs chances de développer l'autisme même si elles ont des mutations dans d'autres gènes. Cela aide à comprendre pourquoi l'autisme est moins fréquent chez les filles et ouvre de nouvelles pistes de recherche.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques doivent faire plus d'expériences pour confirmer comment ZFX protège contre l'autisme. Ils veulent aussi étudier d'autres facteurs comme les hormones ou d'autres gènes. L'objectif est de mieux comprendre les causes de l'autisme et d'améliorer le diagnostic et le traitement.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un gène du chromosome X, ZFX, pourrait protéger les filles de l'autisme en contrôlant d'autres gènes liés à cette condition et en les maintenant actifs.
articles.personality_title_es: Un gen en el cromosoma X podría explicar por qué menos niñas tienen autismo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
